questions.prompt: Where must authorization decisions be enforced?

options.text: On the server, for every request, against the actual object
On the client, by hiding buttons the user shouldn't see

questions.explanation: Authorization must be enforced server-side on every request (complete mediation); hiding UI is not a control because the client can be bypassed.

questions.prompt: Match each access-control model to its description.

pairs.right: The resource owner decides who gets access
A central policy enforces access by labels
Permissions attach to roles assigned to users

questions.explanation: DAC is owner-decided, MAC is label-based and centrally enforced, RBAC uses roles, and ABAC uses attributes and context.

questions.prompt: Accessing another user's object by changing an identifier, with no ownership check, is called ____ (four-letter acronym).
questions.explanation: IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) is fetching a resource by a user-supplied id without verifying the requester owns it.

questions.prompt: Which practices help prevent broken access control? Select all that apply.

options.text: Deny by default and grant explicitly
Verify object ownership on every access
Rely on hiding admin URLs from users

questions.explanation: Deny-by-default, ownership verification, and server-side enforcement prevent broken access control; hidden URLs are obscurity, not access control.

questions.prompt: Order the server-side checks for a request like DELETE /docs/42.

items.text: Verify the object belongs to the user (blocks IDOR)
Check the user's role allows the action

questions.explanation: The server authenticates, verifies ownership of the specific object, checks the role permits the action, and only then performs it.

questions.prompt: Which OWASP Top 10 (2021) category is broken access control, and its rank?

options.text: A01 — ranked #1, the most common serious web risk
It is not in the OWASP Top 10

questions.explanation: Broken Access Control is A01:2021 — the top-ranked web application risk.
